nodes.name: Hydrothermal NiFe-LDH synthesis
nodes.procedure: NiFe-LDH was grown on nickel foam via hydrothermal process. The XRD pattern matched Ni_{0.75}Fe_{0.25}(OH)_2(CO_3)_{0.125}\cdot 0.38H_2O (PDF#40-0215) with sharp (003) peak at ~11° confirming layered structure. Morphology showed typical hexagonal structure.
nodes.source_text: The anode we used is NiFe-LDH grown on nickel foam via a hydrothermal process.[33] The XRD pattern... matched well with Ni_{0.75}Fe_{0.25}(OH)_2(CO_3)_{0.125}\cdot 0.38H_2O (PDF#40-0215)... sharp diffraction peak around 11° corresponds to (003) plane... morphology resembled typical hexagonal structure.

nodes.description: OER LSV screening with 0.25 M halide additives in alkaline simulated seawater (three-electrode)

electrolyte.value: 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl + 0.25 M X-

nodes.source_text: The OER performance of NiFe-LDH was evaluated using a standard three-electrode setup in alkaline simulated seawater (1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl) with different halide additives. As presented in Figure 1b, the addition of 0.25M F- (denoted as NiFe-LDH@F-) and I- (NiFe-LDH@I-) significantly enhanced catalytic activity, with overpotentials at 10 mA cm−2 following the trend: ηNiFe-LDH@I 142 mV < ηNiFe-LDH@F 222 mV < ηNiFe-LDH 251 mV

nodes.description: Chronopotentiometry stability at 500 mA/cm² in high salinity electrolyte with halide additives

electrolyte.value: 1 M KOH + 2.5 M NaCl + 0.25 M X-

nodes.source_text: Chronopotentiometry (CP) provides valuable insight into catalyst stability under practical operating conditions. Pure NiFe-LDH exhibited rapid performance degradation within 2 h under 500 mA cm-2 in 1 M KOH+2.5 M NaCl electrolyte (Figure 1f). ... Remarkably, the addition of F- enabled continuous, corrosion-resistant operation for 24h

nodes.description: F- concentration optimization for OER in simulated seawater

electrolyte.value: 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl + varying F-

nodes.source_text: F- was added as an electrolyte additive with varying concentrations to examine its effect on the OER performance of NiFe-LDH in simulated seawater (1M KOH + 0.5M NaCl) Figures 2a and S8 illustrate that increasing the concentration of F- greatly enhanced the OER activity of NiFe-LDH until reaching its optimum at approximately 0.25M, where η10 was reduced to around 222mV

nodes.description: OER stability at 2 A/cm² in real alkaline seawater with optimized F-
nodes.source_text: Under a current density of 2Acm−2, NiFe-LDH@F maintained stable operation for 1000h, significantly outperforming NiFeLDH, and exhibited no noticeable potential fluctuations (Figure 2g). Similarly, after optimizing the F- concentration, NiFe-LDH achieved stable operation at 2Acm−2 for 1000h in real seawater electrolyte ... exhibiting only 10.8 μV h−1 performance degradation, representing an approximately 500-fold improvement over the unprotected control.

nodes.description: Stepwise NaCl addition corrosion tolerance test at 500 mA/cm²

electrolyte.value: 1 M KOH + stepwise 0.5 M NaCl + 0.25 M F-

nodes.source_text: To identify the maximum Cl- concentration NiFe-LDH@F- could tolerate, a stepwise increase of 0.5M NaCl was added every 4 h into 1M KOH + 0.5M NaCl electrolyte, maintaining operating at 500mAcm-2 (Figure 2e). ... NiFe-LDH@F- exhibited no corrosion until the electrolyte concentration reached 3M NaCl

nodes.description: AEMWE full cell performance with NiFe-LDH anode and NiMo cathode
nodes.source_text: To demonstrate the practical application of direct alkaline seawater electrolysis, we constructed an AEMWE using NiFeLDH as the anode and NiMo alloy as the cathode. As shown in Figure S17, when F- was added as an electrolyte additive, the electrolyzer required applied voltages of only 1.72, 1.88, and 2.11V to achieve current densities of 0.25, 0.5, and 1Acm-2, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD pattern of NiFe-LDH grown on nickel foam matches Ni0.75Fe0.25(OH)2(CO3)0.125·0.38H2O (PDF#40-0215) with sharp (003) peak at ~11° confirming layered structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The XRD pattern of the catalyst grown on nickel foam (Figure S1a) matched well with Ni0.75Fe0.25(OH)2(CO3)0.125·0.38H2O (PDF#40-0215), with slight peak shifts attributed to the different Ni/Fe ratio.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM shows typical hexagonal morphology of NiFe-LDH with well-defined layered structure maintained in presence of F-.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In addition, the morphology resembled the typical hexagonal structure of NiFe-LDH (Figure S1b), further confirming that the obtained material was NiFe-LDH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Double-layer capacitance (Cdl) of NiFe-LDH is 1.66 mF cm^-2, unchanged at 1.74 mF cm^-2 with F- addition.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The introduction of F- did not reduce the Cdl of NiFe-LDH (1.74 mF cm^-2 for NiFe-LDH@F- versus 1.66 mF cm^-2 for NiFe-LDH), suggesting that F- does not hinder the exposure of electroactive sites on NiFe-LDH (Figure 1d).

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS shows charge transfer resistance of 0.229 Ω for NiFe-LDH (0.228 Ω for NiFe-LDH@F-), lower than other halides (0.334 Ω Cl-, 0.237 Ω Br-, 0.244 Ω I-).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis further revealed that F- significantly reduced charge transfer resistance (0.229Ω for NiFe-LDH, 0.228Ω for NiFe-LDH@F-, 0.334Ω for NiFe-LDH@Cl-, 0.237Ω for NiFe-LDH@Br-, and 0.244Ω for NiFe-LDH@I-,) at the electrode interface (Figure 1e and Table S1).

nodes.characterization_summary: High-resolution Ni 2p and Fe 2p XPS peaks shift to higher binding energies after F- treatment, indicating oxidation of Ni and Fe sites to higher valence states.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Figure 3a, the high-resolution Ni 2p XPS peaks were assigned to Ni2+ 2p3/2 and 2p1/2. Compared to the sample without activating in F- contained electrolyte, the Ni 2p signals shifted to higher binding energies after stability test.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman shows NiFe-LDH@F- exhibits peak shifts from 448/522 cm^-1 (Ni2+) to 469/547 cm^-1 (Ni3+) at 1.37 V vs RHE, earlier than F-free NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The NiFe-LDH@F- exhibited a shift of the peaks from 448 and 522 cm^-1 (corresponding to Ni2+ Ni-O bending and stretching vibrations) to 469 and 547 cm^-1 (Ni3+ Ni-O bending and stretching vibrations) at 1.37 V versus RHE.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Bode plots show NiFe-LDH@F- undergoes electrooxidation at 1.42 V and OER initiation at 1.44 V vs RHE, earlier than F-free NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Figure 3f, at 1.42 V versus RHE, the middle-frequency peak dropped sharply for NiFe-LDH@F-, indicating the electrooxidation in NiFe-LDH.

nodes.characterization_summary: TOF-SIMS shows decreased NiCl- and FeCl- signals for NiFe-LDH@F- with stable NiF- and FeF- signals, indicating suppressed Cl- accumulation and metal dissolution.
nodes.evidence_snippet: For pristine NiFeLDH after test in NaCl containing electrolyte, the slight increase in NiCl- and FeCl- signals were observed (Figure 4c, Region I and II), indicating Cl- accumulation and dissolve Ni and Fe.

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-MS confirms F- suppresses Ni dissolution from 18.77 to 10.90 μg L^-1 and Fe from 114.07 to 65.10 μg L^-1.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) was then carried out and confirmed that F- addition suppressed the dissolution of Ni (from 18.77 to 10.90 μg L^-1) and Fe (from 114.07 to 65.10 μg L^-1) from NiFe-LDH (Figure S22).

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman in 2800-3800 cm^-1 range shows NiFe-LDH@F- has higher free H2O (6.98% to 5.80%) and 4-HB-H2O (41.88% to 43.00%) content than F-free NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: At identical applied voltages, the NiFe-LDH@F- exhibited a greater percentage of both free water and 4-HB-H2O (Figure 4a,b) compared to NiFe-LDH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando ATR-IRAS confirms higher 4-HB-H2O content (19.78% at 1.2 V, 25.70% at 1.7 V vs RHE) on NiFe-LDH@F- compared to F-free NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Comparative analysis of 4-HB-H2O (Figure S30a) on NiFe-LDH and NiFe-LDH@F- electrodes revealed that, in the presence of fluoride ions in electrolyte, a higher 4-HB-H2O content (19.78%) was already observed at a lower potential (1.2 V versus RHE).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ion chromatography confirms F- adsorption on NiFe-LDH surface is not fully reversible.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Ion chromatography (Table S5) further confirmed that F- adsorption was not fully reversible, since most F- strongly interacted with the electrode and was not released either after ceasing the applied potential or upon electrolyte replacement.
